items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "suburbanisation".
items.answer: The outward growth of a city as people and businesses move to the suburbs
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the outward growth of a city as people and businesses move to the suburbs. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain the difference between urbanisation and urban growth.
items.answer: Urbanisation is an increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas; urban growth is an increase in the number of urban dwellers or the area covered by cities. A city can grow without urbanisation if the rural population grows equally fast.
items.markingKey: Urbanisation is an increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas; urban growth is an increase in the number of urban dwellers or the area covered by cities. A city can grow without urbanisation if the rural population grows equally fast. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Rafael writes: "Most of the world's urban growth is happening in Europe and North America." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most urban growth now happens in Asia and Africa; HIC cities grow slowly.
items.markingKey: Most urban growth now happens in Asia and Africa; HIC cities grow slowly. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The number of megacities in the world went from 10 megacities in 1990 to 33 megacities in 2018. Which is the percentage change?

Hana argues that "Rapid urbanisation brings more benefits than problems to low-income countries." Kwame disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Urbanisation can drive development, but only if planning and investment in housing, transport and services keep pace; otherwise problems may outweigh benefits for the poorest.
items.markingKey: Hana: cities offer jobs, higher wages, education and health care. Kwame: growth often outpaces housing and services, creating informal settlements. Judgement (1-2 marks): Urbanisation can drive development, but only if planning and investment in housing, transport and services keep pace; otherwise problems may outweigh benefits for the poorest.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "Why has the population of Dhaka grown so rapidly since 1990?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Collect UN population data; graph growth; research push factors (river erosion, flooding) and pull factors (garment industry); read two case studies; evaluate sources; cite in APA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect UN population data; graph growth; research push factors (river erosion, flooding) and pull factors (garment industry); read two case studies; evaluate sources; cite in APA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: In which world regions is urban growth now fastest?
items.answer: Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia
items.markingKey: D. Cities like Lagos, Kinshasa and Dhaka are growing rapidly.

items.stem: Briefly explain why high-income countries have slower urban growth than LICs.
items.answer: They urbanised during industrialisation, so about 80% already live in cities; birth rates are low and some people move out to suburbs and rural areas (counter-urbanisation).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They urbanised during industrialisation, so about 80% already live in cities; birth rates are low and some people move out to suburbs and rural areas (counter-urbanisation). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The data show the population of Dhaka, Bangladesh (UN estimates of the urban agglomeration): 1950: 0.34 million; 1970: 1.4 million; 1990: 6.6 million; 2010: 14.7 million; 2020: 21 million. Calculate the average rate of change per year between 1950 and 2010, and per decade.
items.answer: +0.239 million per year (+2.39 per decade)

items.stem:
Source A – UN report (paraphrased): Summary of United Nations DESA, "World Urbanization Prospects: The 2018 Revision"

The report stated that 55% of the world's population lived in urban areas in 2018 and that this share was projected to rise to 68% by 2050. Close to 90% of the increase in urban population would take place in Asia and Africa, and just three countries – India, China and Nigeria – would account for over a third of the growth.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching urbanisation trends in HICs and LICs and the rise of megacities? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of United Nations DESA, "World Urbanization Prospects: The 2018 Revision". Purpose: to provide data and projections on urbanisation for governments and planners. Value: The UN is the main global source of urban data and uses national censuses. Limitation: Definitions of "urban" vary between countries, and projections may change as birth rates and migration change.
items.markingKey: Origin: Summary of United Nations DESA, "World Urbanization Prospects: The 2018 Revision". Purpose: to provide data and projections on urbanisation for governments and planners. Value: The UN is the main global source of urban data and uses national censuses. Limitation: Definitions of "urban" vary between countries, and projections may change as birth rates and migration change. Award up to [4]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 4), scaled to the marks: 7-8 discusses concepts, issues and theories in detail, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses and evaluates a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and interprets different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: About how many rural migrant workers were there in China in 2023?
items.answer: About 300 million
items.markingKey: About 300 million. China's National Bureau of Statistics reported about 298 million.

items.stem: Briefly explain why climate change may increase rural–urban migration.
items.answer: Droughts, floods and rising seas damage crops and land, reducing rural livelihoods, especially in places such as coastal Bangladesh and the Sahel.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Droughts, floods and rising seas damage crops and land, reducing rural livelihoods, especially in places such as coastal Bangladesh and the Sahel. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "People move to cities only because of pull factors." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most migration results from a combination of push and pull factors and personal circumstances.
items.markingKey: Most migration results from a combination of push and pull factors and personal circumstances. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which migration from Bangladesh's coastal districts to Dhaka shows environmental push factors.
items.answer: River erosion, cyclones and salinisation of farmland push many people to Dhaka, where the garment industry offers jobs. Environmental change combined with urban jobs drives migration.
items.markingKey: Context (River erosion, cyclones and salinisation of farmland push many people to Dhaka, where the garment industry offers jobs.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: environmental change combined with urban jobs drives migration. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to environmental push factors.

items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "What are the main push and pull factors for families who have moved to our city in the last ten years?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Collect census data on migration; interview ten families (with consent); code reasons as push or pull; present in a chart; compare with Lee's model; evaluate ethics and sampling.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect census data on migration; interview ten families (with consent); code reasons as push or pull; present in a chart; compare with Lee's model; evaluate ethics and sampling. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Mateo argues that "Push factors are more important than pull factors in explaining rural–urban migration." Amara disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Both matter: push factors often explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; the balance differs by place and person.
items.markingKey: Mateo: rural poverty, land shortage and climate shocks force many to leave. Amara: cities attract migrants with higher wages and services even when rural life is stable. Judgement (1-2 marks): Both matter: push factors often explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; the balance differs by place and person.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Push factors are more important than pull factors in explaining rural–urban migration."
items.answer: Both matter: push factors often explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; the balance differs by place and person.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rural poverty, land shortage and climate shocks force many to leave; environmental disasters create sudden movement. Arguments against: cities attract migrants with higher wages and services even when rural life is stable; migrant networks pull family members to particular cities. Supported judgement: Both matter: push factors often explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; the balance differs by place and person.

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Push factors are more important than pull factors in explaining rural–urban migration."
items.answer: Thesis: Both matter: push factors often explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; the balance differs by place and person.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rural poverty, land shortage and climate shocks force many to leave; environmental disasters create sudden movement. Counter-arguments: cities attract migrants with higher wages and services even when rural life is stable; migrant networks pull family members to particular cities. Thesis/conclusion: Both matter: push factors often explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; the balance differs by place and person. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Briefly explain why the mechanisation of farming can push people to cities.
items.answer: Machines replace farm labourers, so fewer jobs remain in rural areas and people move to cities to find work.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Machines replace farm labourers, so fewer jobs remain in rural areas and people move to cities to find work. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between forced migration and voluntary migration.
items.answer: Voluntary migration is chosen, usually for economic or family reasons; forced migration happens when people have no real choice, because of conflict, persecution or disaster.
items.markingKey: Voluntary migration is chosen, usually for economic or family reasons; forced migration happens when people have no real choice, because of conflict, persecution or disaster. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: They have fewer family ties, more years to benefit from higher wages, are more likely to be seeking education or a first job, and are more willing to take risks.
items.markingKey: Content: They have fewer family ties, more years to benefit from higher wages, are more likely to be seeking education or a first job, and are more willing to take risks. items.stem: Dharavi, one of Asia's largest informal settlements, is in which city?
items.answer: Mumbai
items.markingKey: A. Up to a million people live in about 2 km².

items.stem: Briefly explain why informal settlements are also places of economic activity.
items.answer: Residents run businesses such as recycling, pottery, garment work and food production; Dharavi's informal economy is estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Residents run businesses such as recycling, pottery, garment work and food production; Dharavi's informal economy is estimated at hundreds of millions of dollars a year. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between the informal economy and the formal economy.
items.answer: The formal economy consists of registered, taxed jobs with contracts and legal protection; the informal economy consists of unregistered work, such as street vending, with no contracts or protection.
items.markingKey: The formal economy consists of registered, taxed jobs with contracts and legal protection; the informal economy consists of unregistered work, such as street vending, with no contracts or protection. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A geography student finds that Nigeria covers 923,768 km² and had about 223.8 million people in 2023. Work out the number of people per square kilometre and show your method.
items.answer: 242 people per km²
items.markingKey: Density = population ÷ area (M1) = 223,800,000 ÷ 923,768 = 242 people per km² (A1). Units required.

items.stem: A student claims: "Everyone in informal settlements is unemployed." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most residents work, often in the informal economy or in low-paid formal jobs; informal settlements are busy economic hubs.
items.markingKey: Most residents work, often in the informal economy or in low-paid formal jobs; informal settlements are busy economic hubs. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe the research methods you would use to answer "How effective has the Favela-Bairro programme been in improving living conditions in Rio de Janeiro's favelas since 1994?", naming specific sources and explaining why each is appropriate.
items.answer: Read programme reports and two academic studies; compare indicators (water, sanitation, crime) before and after; find residents' views in interviews or documentaries; evaluate sources; cite in APA.

items.stem: Define the term "urban heat island".
items.answer: The effect by which cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the effect by which cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Zara writes: "Building more roads will solve traffic congestion." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: New roads often attract more traffic (induced demand); public transport, cycling and land-use planning are usually more effective.
items.markingKey: New roads often attract more traffic (induced demand); public transport, cycling and land-use planning are usually more effective. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why informal settlements grow in rapidly expanding cities.
items.answer: Migrants and low-income residents cannot afford formal housing, and governments cannot build homes and services fast enough, so people build on unused or unsafe land.
items.markingKey: Content: Migrants and low-income residents cannot afford formal housing, and governments cannot build homes and services fast enough, so people build on unused or unsafe land. items.stem: Which country launched its "Smart Nation" initiative in 2014?
items.answer: Singapore
items.markingKey: Singapore. It uses sensors and data for transport and services.

items.stem: "A smart city is automatically a sustainable city." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Technology can improve efficiency, but sustainability also depends on reducing consumption, social equity and green space.
items.markingKey: Technology can improve efficiency, but sustainability also depends on reducing consumption, social equity and green space. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why smart-city technology raises concerns about privacy.
items.answer: Sensors, cameras and apps collect large amounts of data about people's movements and behaviour, which could be misused by governments or companies without strong safeguards.

items.stem: Briefly explain why some planned smart cities have struggled to attract residents.
items.answer: Top-down projects such as Songdo or Masdar were expensive, sometimes far from existing jobs and communities, and built around technology rather than residents' needs.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "push factor"?
options: The movement of people from the countryside to towns and cities
The outward growth of a city as people and businesses move to the suburbs
The effect by which cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas
A negative aspect of a place that encourages people to leave, such as unemployment, drought or conflict
items.answer: A negative aspect of a place that encourages people to leave, such as unemployment, drought or conflict
items.markingKey: D. "push factor" is a negative aspect of a place that encourages people to leave, such as unemployment, drought or conflict.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "urban growth"?
options: An area of housing built without legal permission, often lacking secure tenure, water, sanitation and services
The increase in the number of people living in urban areas, or in the area a city covers
A city that is much larger than any other in its country and dominates its economy and politics, such as Lima or Bangkok
The effect by which cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas
items.answer: The increase in the number of people living in urban areas, or in the area a city covers
items.markingKey: B. "urban growth" is the increase in the number of people living in urban areas, or in the area a city covers.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "urban heat island"?

The effect by which cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas
A negative aspect of a place that encourages people to leave, such as unemployment, drought or conflict
A city that is much larger than any other in its country and dominates its economy and politics, such as Lima or Bangkok
items.answer: The effect by which cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas
items.markingKey: B. "urban heat island" is the effect by which cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a smart city and a sustainable city.
items.answer: A smart city uses digital technology and data to manage services; a sustainable city aims to meet people's needs with low environmental impact. A smart city is not automatically sustainable, and sustainable cities do not need high technology.
items.markingKey: A smart city uses digital technology and data to manage services; a sustainable city aims to meet people's needs with low environmental impact. items.stem: Arjun is investigating urbanisation trends in HICs and LICs and the rise of megacities and proposes the research question: "What is a city?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a definition question with nothing to investigate Improved: "Why has the population of Dhaka grown so rapidly since 1990?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a definition question with nothing to investigate); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "Why has the population of Dhaka grown so rapidly since 1990?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Explain why "How effective has the Favela-Bairro programme been in improving living conditions in Rio de Janeiro's favelas since 1994?" is a suitable research question for an MYP investigation into urban challenges: informal settlements, traffic, pollution and services.
items.answer: It evaluates a real urban management strategy using reports and residents' views.
items.markingKey: It evaluates a real urban management strategy using reports and residents' views. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. items.stem:
Source A – News feature (paraphrased): Paraphrase of international news features on Songdo International Business District, South Korea, 2010s–2020s

The reporter described Songdo as a city of glass towers, parks and pneumatic waste pipes built on reclaimed land. More than a decade after construction began, many apartments were occupied, but some residents said the city felt quiet and lacked the life of older neighbourhoods in Seoul.

Identify two points that Source A makes about planning sustainable cities, including a case study of a smart city, using evidence from the source.
items.answer: Songdo has advanced technology and green space but some residents find it lacks community life.
items.markingKey: Songdo has advanced technology and green space but some residents find it lacks community life. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: A class brainstorm on push and pull factors of rural–urban migration produced the question "Why do people move?" Explain why it needs refining, then suggest an improved research question and justify your change.
items.answer: Weakness: it is too broad and general to investigate with evidence Improved: "What are the main push and pull factors for families who have moved to our city in the last ten years?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is too broad and general to investigate with evidence); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "What are the main push and pull factors for families who have moved to our city in the last ten years?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Rapid urbanisation brings more benefits than problems to low-income countries." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Urbanisation can drive development, but only if planning and investment in housing, transport and services keep pace; otherwise problems may outweigh benefits for the poorest.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: cities offer jobs, higher wages, education and health care; urban economies drive national growth and innovation. Counter-arguments: growth often outpaces housing and services, creating informal settlements; congestion, pollution and inequality increase. Thesis/conclusion: Urbanisation can drive development, but only if planning and investment in housing, transport and services keep pace; otherwise problems may outweigh benefits for the poorest. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: "Upgrading informal settlements is better than replacing them." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Upgrading is usually the better approach where sites are safe, because it improves lives without destroying livelihoods; relocation should be a last resort with residents' consent.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it keeps communities, jobs and social networks in place; it is cheaper and improves conditions quickly, as in Rio's Favela-Bairro programme. Arguments against: some sites are too hazardous to upgrade safely; upgrading may not provide enough space or quality housing. Supported judgement: Upgrading is usually the better approach where sites are safe, because it improves lives without destroying livelihoods; relocation should be a last resort with residents' consent. items.stem: "Smart technology is the best way to make cities sustainable." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Technology helps, but good planning – public transport, mixed-use development, green space and community involvement – matters more than technology itself.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: data can cut energy use, manage traffic and reduce waste; Singapore shows the benefits of integrated technology. Arguments against: low-tech solutions such as Curitiba's BRT and cycling are cheaper and proven; technology can be costly and raise privacy and equity concerns. Supported judgement: Technology helps, but good planning – public transport, mixed-use development, green space and community involvement – matters more than technology itself. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A negative aspect of a place that encourages people to leave, such as unemployment, drought or conflict"?
items.answer: push factor
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of push factor.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities"?
items.answer: urbanisation
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of urbanisation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The effect by which cities are warmer than surrounding rural areas"?
items.answer: urban heat island
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of urban heat island.

items.stem: A student claims: "Sustainable cities must be built from scratch." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Most sustainable change happens by retrofitting existing cities – e.g. Copenhagen's cycle lanes or Seoul's restored Cheonggyecheon stream.
items.markingKey: Most sustainable change happens by retrofitting existing cities – e.g. Copenhagen's cycle lanes or Seoul's restored Cheonggyecheon stream. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Sana writes: "Migration always means moving permanently." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Much rural–urban migration is temporary or circular – e.g. seasonal construction work or returning home for harvests.
items.markingKey: Much rural–urban migration is temporary or circular – e.g. seasonal construction work or returning home for harvests. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between urban growth and urbanisation.
items.answer: Urbanisation is an increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas; urban growth is an increase in the number of urban dwellers or the area covered by cities. A city can grow without urbanisation if the rural population grows equally fast.
items.markingKey: Urbanisation is an increase in the proportion of people living in urban areas; urban growth is an increase in the number of urban dwellers or the area covered by cities. A city can grow without urbanisation if the rural population grows equally fast. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why informal settlements are often built in hazardous locations.
items.answer: Steep slopes, floodplains, rubbish dumps and land beside railways are unwanted by formal developers, so the poorest residents settle there despite the risks of landslides and floods.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Steep slopes, floodplains, rubbish dumps and land beside railways are unwanted by formal developers, so the poorest residents settle there despite the risks of landslides and floods. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between a sustainable city and a smart city.
items.answer: A smart city uses digital technology and data to manage services; a sustainable city aims to meet people's needs with low environmental impact. A smart city is not automatically sustainable, and sustainable cities do not need high technology.
items.markingKey: A smart city uses digital technology and data to manage services; a sustainable city aims to meet people's needs with low environmental impact. A smart city is not automatically sustainable, and sustainable cities do not need high technology. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between a pull factor and a push factor.
items.answer: Push factors drive people away from where they live (unemployment, drought, conflict); pull factors attract them to a destination (jobs, services, family networks).
items.markingKey: Push factors drive people away from where they live (unemployment, drought, conflict); pull factors attract them to a destination (jobs, services, family networks). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

The report stated that 55% of the world's population lived in urban areas in 2018 and that this share was projected to rise to 68% by 2050. Close to 90% of the increase in urban population would take place in Asia and Africa, and just three countries – India, China and Nigeria – would account for over a third of the growth.

items.stem: Using Singapore's Smart Nation as an example, explain a smart city approach.
items.answer: Singapore uses electronic road pricing, sensors and open data to manage traffic, energy and water, alongside extensive green space ("City in Nature"). Technology and strict planning help a dense city remain efficient and liveable.
items.markingKey: Context (Singapore uses electronic road pricing, sensors and open data to manage traffic, energy and water, alongside extensive green space ("City in Nature").) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: technology and strict planning help a dense city remain efficient and liveable. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a smart city approach.

items.stem:
Source A – Survey report (paraphrased): Summary of findings of studies of migration to Dhaka by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and Bangladeshi researchers, 2010s

A survey of newly arrived migrants in Dhaka found that most had moved for economic reasons – especially to find work in the garment sector – but many also named river erosion, floods or loss of land as reasons for leaving their villages. Most sent part of their earnings back to their families.

What is the message of Source A about push and pull factors of rural–urban migration? Refer to details in the source.
items.answer: Migrants to Dhaka move mainly for work, but environmental losses also push them, and many send remittances home.

items.stem:
Source A – Survey report (paraphrased): Summary of findings of studies of migration to Dhaka by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and Bangladeshi researchers, 2010s

A survey of newly arrived migrants in Dhaka found that most had moved for economic reasons – especially to find work in the garment sector – but many also named river erosion, floods or loss of land as reasons for leaving their villages. Most sent part of their earnings back to their families.

Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the claim that "Push factors are more important than pull factors in explaining rural–urban migration."
items.answer: Both matter: push factors often explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; the balance differs by place and person.
items.markingKey: From the source: Migrants to Dhaka move mainly for work, but environmental losses also push them, and many send remittances home. Own knowledge for: rural poverty, land shortage and climate shocks force many to leave; environmental disasters create sudden movement. Own knowledge against: cities attract migrants with higher wages and services even when rural life is stable; migrant networks pull family members to particular cities. Judgement: Both matter: push factors often explain why people leave, but pull factors and networks explain where they go; the balance differs by place and person. items.stem:
Source A – UN-Habitat report (paraphrased): Summary of UN-Habitat, "World Cities Report" and slum indicators, 2020–2022

The report defines a slum household as one lacking one or more of the following: improved water, improved sanitation, durable housing, sufficient living area, or security of tenure. It estimates that over a billion people live in such conditions, mostly in Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into urban challenges: informal settlements, traffic, pollution and services, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Summary of UN-Habitat, "World Cities Report" and slum indicators, 2020–2022. Purpose: to measure urban poverty and guide policy towards the Sustainable Development Goals. Value: It provides a clear, internationally agreed definition and global estimates. Limitation: Measuring informal settlements is difficult and estimates depend on national data quality.
